288.title: One hand
288.hook: Hakuin's koan: you know the sound of two hands; what is the sound of one
288.howItsDone: In Japanese Rinzai Zen, Hakuin's 'sound of one hand' is one of the first koans a teacher may assign, often alongside or instead of mu, followed by a series of checking questions in private interviews.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ordinary mind, and that was your line. Did one plain task get done as if it were the whole Way? Day two hundred eighty-eight.

You've heard it. Probably in a cartoon, or a sitcom, or from a friend being clever at a party: what's the sound of one hand clapping? It's become a punch line, shorthand for a question so deep it's silly. Somebody usually waves one hand in the air, and everybody laughs. But the question has a real home, and a real author. He was a Japanese monk who lived in a small, poor temple at the foot of Mount Fuji, painted wild ink pictures, and nearly broke his own health with practice when he was young. Today: one hand.
screen: `A PUNCH LINE AT A PARTY.` → `ONE HAND WAVED IN THE AIR.` → `A REAL HOME, A REAL AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: His name was Hakuin Ekaku, and he lived from 1686 to 1769. He's remembered as the teacher who revived Rinzai Zen in Japan when it had grown sleepy. Almost every Rinzai teacher in Japan today traces their line through him. For years Hakuin gave his students mu, Zhaozhou's dog, as their first koan. Then, late in life, he started giving them a question of his own. In a letter written in his late sixties, he explains it roughly like this: clap two hands together and there's a sound. What is the sound of one hand? He wrote that he'd found this question raised the great doubt in students more easily than mu. Notice what the koan does to you. The thinking mind reaches for an answer and finds nothing to grab. One hand makes no sound; any fool knows that. So what is he asking? The koan pushes attention toward listening itself, toward what's here before any sound, the silence that every sound comes out of and goes back into. Students work with it for months, sometimes years, and teachers follow up with more questions: hear the sound of one hand from the soles of your feet, or stop the sound of one hand. Hakuin never meant it as a joke, but he had a big sense of humor; his paintings of monks and gods are full of it. He'd probably laugh at the party version too. Then he'd ask you to listen.
screen: `HAKUIN, WHO REVIVED RINZAI.` · `AFTER YEARS OF MU.` · `TWO HANDS MAKE A SOUND.` · `LISTENING ITSELF.` · then, large: `ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and close your eyes if you like. First, just listen to whatever sounds are here: traffic, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Then notice the silence those sounds rise out of and fall back into. Rest your attention there. If you'd like, lift one hand a little and hold it in the air, and ask: what is the sound of this? Don't answer. Just listen. The bell holds the time.
One hand. Hakuin's koan: two hands clap and there's a sound; what is the sound of one hand?
Your line: one hand. Today, find one minute of quiet, even in a noisy place, and listen for what's under the noise. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

what it means: a koan that turns attention to listening itself, before any sound.
what a scholar hears: Hakuin describes it in a letter of the 1750s, and his heirs built the Rinzai koan curriculum that still starts many students with it or with mu.

289.title: Carrying a koan
289.hook: Rinzai students hold a koan all day and bring it to the teacher in private
289.howItsDone: Rinzai Zen students receive a koan from their teacher, hold it in sitting and daily work, and present their response in private interviews called dokusan or sanzen, several times a day during retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one hand, and your line, one hand. Did you find a minute of quiet under the noise? Day two hundred eighty-nine.

A song gets stuck in your head. Nobody decides to keep it. It just rides along: in the shower, on the drive, while you're answering email, humming underneath everything else. Koan practice does that on purpose, not with a song, but with a question like mu or the sound of one hand. Letting it ride along through breakfast, work, the walk home, until it's humming underneath everything. For two weeks you've been reading koans. Today: how people actually practice with them. It isn't in an armchair.
screen: `A SONG STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.` → `NOT IN AN ARMCHAIR.`

segments.voice: In Rinzai Zen, a student doesn't pick a koan off a shelf. The teacher gives it, usually mu or the sound of one hand to begin. Then the student carries it. In sitting meditation, the koan is the whole practice: not thinking about it, but becoming absorbed in it, breath after breath. And then, the part that surprises people, it doesn't stay on the cushion. The student takes it to the kitchen, to the garden, to the walk between buildings. Hakuin, from yesterday, taught that practice in the middle of activity is far stronger than practice in stillness. Korean Seon teachers say the same about the hwadu: hold it while walking, standing, sitting and lying down. Several times a day during a retreat, and regularly the rest of the year, the student goes alone to the teacher's room. This private meeting is called dokusan or sanzen. The student bows and presents the koan, not with an explanation but with a response, sometimes a word, a gesture, a silence. Often the teacher rings a small hand bell and the meeting is over: not yet, go back and keep going. Some students hear that bell for months. By custom, what happens in the room stays in the room. Students don't share their answers, and that's one reason the published books of answers that circulate miss the point: a response only counts if it comes from you, in the moment, face to face. When a student finally passes the first koan, the work isn't over. Many more follow, each opening the first seeing a little wider.
screen: `THE TEACHER GIVES THE KOAN.` · `OFF THE CUSHION, INTO THE DAY.` · `ALONE IN THE TEACHER'S ROOM.` · `A SMALL BELL: NOT YET.` · then, large: `CARRY IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring back mu, the first koan, and let it ride the out-breath, the way you did eleven days ago. Mu. Not thinking about it. Just the sound, all the way out. Then imagine standing up and carrying it into one chore: the dishes, folding clothes, walking to the mailbox. Mu with each step, each plate. After the bell, you're invited to try it for real, for one chore. The bell holds the time.
Carrying a koan. In Rinzai practice, the koan goes everywhere with you, and you bring your response to the teacher alone.
Your line: carry it. Today, take one question you care about and let it ride along through an ordinary task, without forcing an answer. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: What koans are not
290.hook: not riddles with clever answers; Soto Zen stresses just sitting instead, and both are Zen
290.howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit shikantaza, usually facing a wall, without a koan; in Rinzai Zen they usually sit facing into the room and work with koans. Some lineages teach both.

segments.voice: Yesterday: carrying a koan, and your line, carry it. Did a question ride along through a chore? Day two hundred ninety, the last day of the koans.

After two weeks of dogs, bowls, foxes, fingers, flags, flowers, faces, cats, good days and one hand, you might think Zen is basically koans. Step into a Soto Zen hall in Japan and there's something different. People sitting facing a plain wall. No question to hold. No interview bell. Just sitting, for a long time, very still. That's Zen too. Today we close the koans by saying what they aren't, and by meeting the other great way Zen is practiced.
screen: `DOGS, BOWLS, FOXES, FLAGS.` → `PEOPLE FACING A PLAIN WALL.` → `THAT'S ZEN TOO.`

segments.voice: First, what koans are not. They're not riddles with clever answers; the teacher's bell sends clever answers back. They're not nonsense meant to confuse you; each one grew out of a real encounter and points somewhere. And they're not the only way to practice Zen. In Japan the two main Zen schools are Rinzai, which you've been meeting, and Soto. Soto was brought from China by a Japanese monk named Dogen. Dogen's teacher in China had a phrase for the heart of practice: just sitting. In Japanese, shikantaza. You sit upright, usually facing a wall, eyes half open, and you don't hold a koan, count breaths or aim at anything. You just sit, fully awake to sitting. Remember nothing to attain, back in the Heart Sutra: Dogen taught that sitting isn't a means to awakening later. Sitting is awakening, being expressed. The difference isn't new. Back in Song-dynasty China, one teacher, Dahui, championed working on a single koan phrase, while another, Hongzhi, taught a quiet practice he called silent illumination. They disagreed, and were friends: tradition says Hongzhi asked Dahui to handle his funeral. Today, Rinzai teachers stress koans, Soto teachers stress just sitting, and both schools say the other is Zen. Soto teachers study koans too; Dogen wrote about them often. And some lineages, especially in the West, teach both. Two weeks of koans, closed in silence: don't solve it, mu, wash your bowl, not blind to cause, your own finger, mind moves, the smile, before you were born, sandals on the head, every day is a good day, ordinary mind, one hand, carry it. And now, just sitting.
screen: `NOT RIDDLES, NOT NONSENSE.` · `SOTO ZEN AND DOGEN.` · `SHIKANTAZA: JUST SITTING.` · `DAHUI AND HONGZHI, FRIENDS.` · then, large: `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: For this sit, no koan, no counting, no word on the breath. Sit upright, as if a thread were lifting the crown of your head. Let your eyes rest half open on the floor or a wall a little in front of you. Now just sit. When thoughts come, don't follow them and don't push them away. Let them pass like weather. Just this body, sitting, breathing. If you'd like more after the bell, try ten minutes this way. The bell holds the time.
What koans are not: riddles, nonsense, or the only way. Soto Zen's just sitting, shikantaza, is Zen too.
Your line: just sitting. Today, sit somewhere for one minute doing nothing else: no phone, no plan, just sitting. Day two hundred ninety.

291.title: The way of the elders
291.hook: the Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with the Pali canon as scripture
291.howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks walk an alms round at dawn, lay people offer food and visit temples on full-moon days, and the Pali canon is chanted in the original language in daily services.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the koans with your line, just sitting. Did you sit for one minute doing nothing else? Day two hundred ninety-one, and a new part of the path: the way of the elders.

Dawn in Luang Prabang, in Laos. A line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot down a quiet street, bowls held in front of them. People kneel on mats by the curb and place a little sticky rice in each bowl. No one speaks. The same thing is happening, more or less, in towns across Thailand, Myanmar and Cambodia, and in a different form in Sri Lanka. Tradition says it has gone on for many centuries. For more than three weeks you've been with the Heart Sutra and Zen. For the next two, you're going south and west, into the school that names itself for the elders.
screen: `DAWN IN LUANG PRABANG.` → `MONKS, BOWLS, STICKY RICE.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR THE ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Theravada. Thera means an elder, a senior monk. Vāda means a teaching, a way of speaking. The teaching of the elders. The name carries a claim: this is the Buddha's teaching as the senior monks remembered and recited it after his death, kept as closely as possible ever since. Theravada is the main Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with communities in Bangladesh, southern Vietnam, and cities all over the world. Its scripture is the Pali canon, written in Pali, an ancient Indian language close to the ones the Buddha spoke. How did it get south? The Sri Lankan chronicles tell it this way. The Indian emperor Ashoka, whose own inscriptions speak of his remorse after a bloody war, sent his own son, a monk named Mahinda, to the king of Sri Lanka. The king listened and became a follower. Ashoka's daughter, the nun Sanghamitta, came later, bringing a branch of the tree the Buddha sat under. Tradition says a tree grown from it still stands at Anuradhapura, where pilgrims honor it today. Later, the chronicle says, monks in Sri Lanka wrote the canon down for the first time, fearing it could be lost. Later it traveled to Southeast Asia. Theravada Buddhists and Mahayana Buddhists share the core, the four truths, the eightfold path, the three refuges. Where they differ, we'll say who says what. For now: the way of the elders, still walking at dawn.
screen: `THERA: ELDER. VĀDA: TEACHING.` · `FIVE COUNTRIES AND THE WORLD.` · `ASHOKA SENDS HIS SON.` · `WRITTEN DOWN ON PALM LEAVES.` · then, large: `THE WAY OF THE ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture a map. Start with India, the Buddha's home. Move down to the island at its tip, Sri Lanka. Then east across the sea: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia. Picture, in each place, a line of monks at dawn and someone kneeling with a bowl of rice. Let your breath move with them, slow and quiet. After the bell, if you'd like, find those five countries on a real map. The bell holds the time.
Theravada. The teaching of the elders: the Buddhism of Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia, with the Pali canon as its scripture.
Your line: the way of the elders. Today, think of one thing an elder in your life taught you that you still do, and do it on purpose. Day two hundred ninety-one.

292.title: Three baskets
292.hook: discipline, discourses, and the higher teaching: the Pali canon
292.howItsDone: Theravada monks memorize and chant passages from the three baskets, recite the monastic rules every two weeks, and in Myanmar monks can sit formal exams on the canon.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Theravada, and your line, the way of the elders. Did you do one thing an elder taught you, on purpose? Day two hundred ninety-two.

In Mandalay, in Myanmar, there's a pagoda surrounded by small white shrines, row after row, like a quiet city. Inside each one stands a marble slab, taller than a person, carved on both sides with tiny letters. Walk them all and you've walked through a book. A Burmese king had the whole scripture of his tradition carved in stone, slab after slab, so it would outlast palm leaves and paper. A book made of marble. What's carved on those slabs comes in three parts. Today: the three baskets.
screen: `A CITY OF WHITE SHRINES.` → `MARBLE SLABS, BOTH SIDES CARVED.` → `A BOOK MADE OF MARBLE.`

segments.voice: Tipitaka. Ti, three. Piṭaka, basket. The three baskets. Nobody is completely sure why baskets. One old explanation pictures workers on a building site, passing baskets of earth from hand to hand down a line, the way the teaching was passed down from teacher to student by memory before it was written. The first basket is the Vinaya, the discipline. It holds the rules for monks and nuns, and, charmingly, the stories behind them: what happened that made the Buddha say, from now on, don't do that. The second basket is the Suttas, the discourses: the Buddha's talks and conversations, gathered into five collections, the long ones, the middle-length ones, the connected ones grouped by topic, the numbered ones grouped by how many items they list, and a fifth collection of shorter works. That fifth one holds the Dhammapada, which this path has quoted before. One of its verses sums up the whole in Max Müller's English: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." The third basket is the Abhidhamma, the higher teaching: seven books that analyze the mind and experience into their tiniest moments, like a chemistry of consciousness. Theravada Buddhists study it seriously, and in Myanmar it's especially honored. Printed, the three baskets fill a long shelf. A British scholar, T. W. Rhys Davids, founded the Pali Text Society to publish and translate them, and his own translations are among those this path draws on.
screen: `TI: THREE. PIṬAKA: BASKET.` · `VINAYA: THE DISCIPLINE.` · `SUTTAS: THE DISCOURSES.` · `ABHIDHAMMA: THE HIGHER TEACHING.` · then, large: `THREE BASKETS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. On the first breath, name the first basket silently: discipline. How you live. On the second: discourses. What the Buddha taught. On the third: the higher teaching. How the mind works, moment by moment. Then go around again, slowly: discipline, discourses, higher teaching. When they feel familiar, let the names go, and just notice this moment of mind, the one the third basket is trying to describe. The bell holds the time.
Tipitaka. The three baskets of the Pali canon: the discipline, the discourses, and the higher teaching.
Your line: three baskets. Today, notice one moment where how you live, what you've learned, and what your mind is doing all meet. Day two hundred ninety-two.

293.title: The forest monks
293.hook: the Thai forest tradition: monks in the jungle, keeping the old rules closely
293.howItsDone: In Thai forest monasteries in Thailand and abroad, monks eat one meal a day from the alms bowl, practice walking and sitting meditation, and keep the monastic rules strictly; lay visitors often come to stay and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tipitaka, and your line, three baskets. Did how you live, what you know and what your mind was doing meet in one moment? Day two hundred ninety-three.

Think about how much of the Buddha's life happened under trees. He was born, the story goes, in a grove, his mother holding a branch. He woke up under a tree. He gave his first teaching in a deer park. He died lying between two trees in a forest. The early monks lived in forests, slept at the roots of trees, and walked into villages only to collect food. Over the centuries, many monasteries moved into towns and cities, and that's natural. But about a hundred years ago, in the northeast of Thailand, a handful of monks walked back into the jungle.
screen: `BORN IN A GROVE.` → `AWAKE UNDER A TREE.` → `BACK INTO THE JUNGLE.`

segments.voice: The best-known of them was Ajahn Mun, born in 1870 in the region of Thailand called Isan, near the Lao border. Ajahn means teacher. With his own teacher, Ajahn Sao, he chose a hard life: wandering on foot through the forests of Thailand and Laos, sleeping under a cloth tent hung with a mosquito net, meditating through the night, and keeping the monastic rules as closely as the old texts describe. The forests then were full of tigers, snakes and malaria. The practice even has an old name, dhutanga, a set of voluntary austerities listed in the commentaries: eating one meal a day, eating only from the bowl, living at the foot of a tree. Monks who took up the wandering life were called thudong monks, from that word. Ajahn Mun trained a generation of students. One of them, Ajahn Chah, founded a forest monastery in 1954 near the city of Ubon, and later a monastery for foreign monks. Through his students, forest monasteries now stand in England, Australia, New Zealand, the United States and beyond, where monks still walk for alms in the morning. Ajahn Chah liked to compare a trained mind to a still pool in the forest, where all kinds of wild animals come to drink, and you can watch them clearly. Most of the forests Ajahn Mun walked through have since been cut down. The monasteries became islands of trees. And the tradition keeps a simple conviction: the Buddha's teaching began in the forest, and the forest remembers.
screen: `AJAHN MUN WALKS INTO THE FOREST.` · `DHUTANGA: THE OLD AUSTERITIES.` · `AJAHN CHAH AND THE STILL POOL.` · `MONASTERIES AS ISLANDS OF TREES.` · then, large: `THE FOREST REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture a forest monastery. A clearing among tall trees. A simple wooden hall, open on the sides. A swept path where a monk walks slowly back and forth. Cicadas, a distant bird. It's early; the air is cool. Now let the picture fade and imagine your own mind as a still forest pool. Thoughts come to drink, like animals at the edge. You don't chase them. You watch. The bell holds the time.
The forest monks. The Thai forest tradition of Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah: monks in the woods, keeping the old rules closely.
Your line: the forest remembers. Today, spend a few minutes near a tree, any tree, and let it remind you where this path began. Day two hundred ninety-three.

294.title: The 227 rules
294.hook: a fully ordained monk keeps 227 rules, a nun more; rules as a shelter
294.howItsDone: Theravada monks keep the 227 rules of the Pāṭimokkha, confess lapses to one another and recite the rules together every new and full moon; lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and eight on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the forest monks, and your line, the forest remembers. Did you spend a few minutes near a tree? Day two hundred ninety-four, the end of the week.

Most of us have a complicated relationship with rules. Speed limits, dress codes, the terms and conditions nobody reads. Rules can feel like a fence someone else built around you. A Theravada monk chooses, freely, to live by two hundred twenty-seven of them. Not eating after noon. Not touching money. Not digging in the ground. Not sleeping in a luxurious bed. That's the life of a fully ordained monk, and some keep it for their whole lives. Why would anyone want that? The answer the tradition gives changes what a rule is.
screen: `SPEED LIMITS AND DRESS CODES.` → `TWO HUNDRED TWENTY-SEVEN, BY CHOICE.` → `WHAT A RULE IS.`

segments.voice: Vinaya means discipline, or training. It's the first of yesterday's three baskets. At its center is a list called the Pāṭimokkha: two hundred twenty-seven rules for monks in the Theravada tradition, and three hundred eleven for fully ordained nuns. Four are the gravest, called defeats: sexual intercourse, stealing, killing a human being, and falsely claiming spiritual attainments. Break one and you're no longer a monk. Most of the rest are small, and many have wonderful origin stories. The rule against digging the ground exists because of the small creatures living in the soil. Every two weeks, on the new moon and the full moon, the monks of a monastery gather, confess any lapses to each other, and one of them recites the whole list aloud. The Vinaya gives the Buddha's own reasons for making rules, ten of them, including the well-being of the community, its ease, restraint for the difficult, and the confidence of people who see monks living well. So the rules work less like a fence and more like a shelter: they keep the weather out so the practice can happen inside. About nuns: in Sri Lanka the Theravada line of fully ordained nuns died out centuries ago. In recent decades, ordinations have revived it, and some Sri Lankan and Western Theravadins recognize those nuns. The official monastic councils of Thailand and Myanmar do not yet. Look back at the week. One hand. Carry it. Just sitting. The way of the elders. Three baskets. The forest remembers. And rules as a shelter.
